summary: The note is a long encyclopedia-style overview of immortality, covering its scientific prospects (anti-aging, biological immortality, telomerase, nanotechnology, cryonics, mind uploading, cybernetics) and its religious conceptions across Christianity, Islam, Judaism, and Dharmic religions. It explains causes of death (aging, disease, trauma, resource limits) and notes that biologically immortal organisms such as bacteria, Turritopsis dohrnii and Hydra exist, while human immortality remains unrealized. The religious sections describe differing views on whether the soul is immortal and on resurrection and afterlife. The text is partly truncated at the Hinduism section.
one_line: Overview of immortality across biology, technology such as cryonics and mind uploading, and major world religions' views on soul, resurrection and afterlife.
key_facts: Biological immortality is defined as an absence of aging, meaning no sustained increase in mortality rate as a function of chronological age.
The first and still most widely used immortal cell line is HeLa, developed from cells taken from Henrietta Lacks without her consent in 1951.
Leonard Hayflick's 1961 work challenged the erroneous belief fostered by Alexis Carrel that all normal somatic cells are immortal.
Telomerase is an enzyme which rebuilds telomeres in stem cells and cancer cells, allowing them to replicate an infinite number of times.
Mice genetically engineered to produce 10 times the normal levels of telomerase lived 50% longer than normal mice, according to researchers at the Spanish National Cancer Centre (Madrid).
Peter Medawar formulated the mutation accumulation theory in 1952 to explain how evolution would select for aging.
Thomas Kirkwood proposed the disposable soma theory in 1977.
Raymond Kurzweil stated in The Singularity Is Near that advanced medical nanorobotics could completely remedy the effects of aging by 2030.
K. Eric Drexler postulated cell repair devices in his 1986 book Engines of Creation.
Cryonics uses vitrification, a process creating a glass-like state rather than freezing, to reduce the risk of ice crystals damaging cell structure.
Aubrey de Grey defines aging as a collection of cumulative changes to the molecular and cellular structure of an adult organism.
Turritopsis dohrnii can transform itself back into a polyp through transdifferentiation after becoming a sexually mature adult.
The note states that the Quran repudiates rejuvenation and physical immortality.
The note states that the traditional concept of an immaterial, immortal soul was not found in Judaism before the Babylonian exile.
